the field is static because the hook it satisfies is static-abstract - ILevelGroupedHooks is implemented by a struct whose members are static, so no Hooks instance exists that could own the result buffer, and no restructuring of the hook can create one (the traversal takes THooks as a static-interface-generic parameter). What makes the sharing safe is AsyncLocal, not the field's placement: the list belongs to the flow that called Walk, LevelGroupedBreadthFirstTraversal runs to completion on that flow, and a second traversal started on another thread writes its own flow's list, never this one's - the same confinement the async-local hook buffers elsewhere in this tier rely on. The mutable-container half of the rule still sees the List, so the reason is recorded here rather than in the source, which this repository's markers policy (safety-only) refuses.

check-responsibility-extraction's own doc (shared-prefix-signals-a-hidden-module.md) calls a prefix cluster a review rather than an automatic defect - 'a prefix cluster is a strong signal, not proof' - and asks the reader to judge whether the shared prefix names a real responsibility before extracting. `Try` names no responsibility here: it is the attempt-returns-success shape of the BCL itself (TryParse, TryGetValue), and this check's own conventional-prefix table already rules the sibling shapes `Is`, `Has`, `Get`, `Set`, `Must` and `With` to be conventions rather than modules for exactly that reason - `Try` is simply absent from that table, which is why this fires. The four counted declarations (TryPeekFront, TryPeekBack, TryPopFront, TryPopBack) are the deque's entire peek/pop surface: this file's own header records that a throwing PeekFront/PopFront is deliberately absent, because emptiness is state an external caller cannot always know in advance, so the TryX forms are the only public way to read the ends - and the type's whole public surface is 7 declarations (Count, PushFront, PushBack and those four), all of one subject. Extracting them would carry the only access path to that subject away from the private buffer that implements it.

same precedent as Deque.cs's own check-responsibility-extraction waiver: 'Try' is the attempt-returns-success convention of the BCL (TryParse, TryGetValue), not a hidden module. The nesting runs inward - Get, Set, Insert and RemoveAt each call their own TryX and throw only when it answers false - so each pair is one validity check under two calling conventions, and splitting the TryX into another file would carry the only copy of that check away from the four members that throw on it. This file's own header records why both forms exist here at all: an out-of-range index is an internal-trusted caller's bug rather than state an external caller cannot know in advance, so throwing loudly beats silently discarding a TryGet result at every internal call site. The paired >8-public-members finding is the same fact: minimal indexed-access API is inherently throwing-form/Try-form x get/set/insert/remove, landing at 9 members without accidental sprawl.

each ! is Floyd's tortoise-and-hare's own invariant, named inline as a `presumption: allow` comment beside each site and recorded here too since the default marker policy only honours safety-critical checks: head! in FindCycleStart is safe because FindMeetingPoint only returns non-null after its walk advanced at least once, which requires a non-null head; fromHead.Next!/fromMeetingPoint.Next! are safe because every node walked from head must reach the cycle FindMeetingPoint already proved exists (a singly linked node has exactly one successor, no branch off that path) and .Next never terminates once inside a cycle; slow! is safe because fast always leads slow by construction (two steps per iteration vs. one), so the loop condition proving fast/fast.Next non-null already proves slow reached that same position non-null on an earlier or equal iteration.

the 6-parameter Search overload (state plus 5 delegates) is a deliberate ergonomic surface, not an accidental one - its own doc comment explains why: it exists specifically so exhaustive-enumeration callers (Subsets, Permutations, N-Queens counting) get a void onSolution and can't accidentally truncate their own search by returning the wrong bool, the exact footgun the canonical BacktrackingSteps<TState,TChoice>-based overload's bool-returning OnSolution invites. Collapsing this overload's parameters into a record struct, as the mechanical fix suggests, would just move that same footgun back onto every caller of this overload - the same 'this broad surface is the type's actual minimum complete API' shape Deque.cs's own check-responsibility-extraction waiver already establishes for a structurally-necessary parameter/member count.

the shared 'Compute' prefix across ComputeOddRadii/ComputeEvenRadii's 4 overload declarations is not a hidden module - it names the one algorithm's two inseparable halves. Manacher's algorithm computes odd- and even-centered palindrome radii by the same technique, and FindLongestPalindromicSubstring genuinely needs both results together to answer 'what is the single longest palindrome' (an odd-only or even-only palindrome could each independently be the answer). Splitting them into separate files would fragment one cohesive technique into two files that always get called together, the same 'this broad surface is the type's actual minimum complete API' shape Deque.cs's own check-responsibility-extraction waiver already establishes.

DescendOneLevel's ! promises the same-bit child is present once the opposite child is absent - true because every node reached mid-walk already has >=1 non-null child by construction (every Insert walks all 32 levels before returning, and Walk is only ever called once Count > 0), so 'opposite absent' plus 'at least one child exists' forces 'same-bit present' by elimination between exactly two possible children; named inline as a `presumption: allow` comment, recorded here too since the default marker policy only honours safety-critical checks.

deliberately flat, one-folder-per-LeetCode-problem layout - each problem is an independent coverage proof against a named, numbered external problem (not a shared subsystem this repo owns the shape of), so there is no real subsystem/contract-surface/role grouping to organize by that wouldn't be arbitrary; the flat list itself is the useful index (a reader scanning for 'is problem X covered' wants to see every problem name at one glance, not one level down inside a hand-picked category).

lca! promises FindLca found an ancestor - true because both queried values come from FindNode walking the same tree FindLca's own root parameter roots, so LowestCommonAncestor.Find always has both nodes reachable from root and can only return null when neither is (impossible here). tree.Root! promises BuildClassicExampleTree's tree is non-empty - true because the method always inserts nine values before returning. Re-measured against the unsuppressed source, not assumed. This entry supersedes two earlier shapes: the DSAExperimentation.Tests/LeetCodeCoverage/** glob, which was measured to carry 505 findings of its own, and the 63 per-file check-literals entries that sat under this tree - 64 suppressions consolidated into 1, not a widening of an empty one. Unsuppressed, DSAExperimentation.Tests holds 2545 check-literals findings across 191 files; production holds zero (DSAExperimentation, DSAExperimentation.LeetCode and DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks all report none). [Re-measured 2026-09-15 against this tree: Tests now holds 2384 findings across 189 files, so the counts just above are the ones taken when this entry was written and later edits moved them. The parenthetical was true of the tree this entry was written against and is not true of this one - with the ledger set aside, DSAExperimentation.LeetCode carries 944 findings across 217 files and DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks 187 across 115, each absorbed by the separate entry written for it. DSAExperimentation itself still reports none.] All 2545 were classified by the line each sits on. 2471 are plainly the test's own data: a literal building the fixture under test (new BinaryTreeNode<int>(1) { Left = new(2) }), an expected value inside an assertion (Assert.Equal(2, children.Count)), a row of theory data, or the prose of an assertion message (Tier5WitnessTests.cs:146). The other 74 are the only shapes that could be a genuine magic number in a test - 68 findings across 44 lines that carry a loop or a branch, and 6 findings across 4 lines whose literal is a float - and none of them is one. The 68 are repetition counts (for (var i = 0; i < 200; i++) paired with Assert.Equal(200, storage.Count)), a domain range (ImplementRand10UsingRand7Tests' for (var value = 1; value <= 10; value++)), the problem's own dimensions (SudokuSolverTests' 9 for the 9x9 board and 3 for one box), or a data vector a foreach walks (BinarySearchTreeTests' foreach (var value in new[] { 5, 3, 8, 1, 4, 7, 9 })). The 6 floats are the values under test (ByPriorityOrderTests' 0.5 and 1.5, LeetCodeAnswersTests' WithinTolerance(0.25, 0.2500001)). Two shapes make naming actively harmful. (a) An assertion's expected value IS the claim the test makes: Assert.Equal("123456789", ...) in SudokuSolverTests is what 'complete and valid' means, and Assert.Equal(26, StandardAlphabets.LowercaseLatin.Characters.Length) proves the alphabet holds 26 characters. Lifting either into a constant satisfies the check by making the test compare a constant with itself, destroying the only thing it proves; and a BoardSize = 9 extracted while the "123456789" that defines the board stays inline would desynchronise two numbers that must agree. (b) Where the literal is an assertion's own message text, a name would restate a sentence as an identifier. The loop-bound minority has a measured counter-argument rather than a fix: a method-local const raises check-constant-scope ('a constant declared inside one function says the number belongs to that function - lift it to module scope'), the 14-new-findings regression measured on SegmentTreeTests this campaign.

the two flagged `2` literals in FillMirroredHalf are `length / 2` (halving a length) and `length % 2 == 1` (odd-length parity check) - the mathematical divisor/modulus for 'half' and 'odd', not an arbitrary business constant. A named constant (e.g. `Two`) would restate the literal without adding information.

IsOneApart(a, b) is a symmetric predicate - Hamming distance is a metric, so d(a,b) == d(b,a) and transposing the two arguments cannot change the result. The check's premise, that a caller can silently get a wrong answer by swapping adjacent same-typed parameters, does not hold for a symmetric relation, and wrapping either side in a distinct type would state a directionality this predicate does not have. The neighbouring OneCharacterMutations(value, alphabet), where transposition IS meaningful, was fixed properly instead by introducing the Alphabet type.

The check asks that a visible constant be moved to 'a type of its own whose subject IS these values'. ModularArithmetic is already that type: the modulus is not incidental state inside a class about something else, it is the single value the whole type is parameterised by, and both public operations (Inverse, Power) are defined only with respect to it. Extracting Modulo to a separate type would leave ModularArithmetic unable to state what it is arithmetic modulo of, in the one file a reader would look in.

The `2` is Factorial's loop start: 0! and 1! are both 1, so multiplication only has to begin at 2. It is the arithmetic's own identity boundary and means nothing but itself - naming it (FirstNonIdentityFactor) would add a constant whose definition is strictly less clear than the literal it replaces.

LockWheels IS the remedy this check prescribes - it was extracted from LockGraph in this same pass precisely because the check asked for 'a type of its own, in its own file whose subject IS these values'. Count/Modulus/CombinationSpace are the lock's dimensions and the entire subject of the type and file; there is no further type to move them to. Same shape as the ModularArithmetic.Modulo waiver.

The check reads a shared method-name prefix as a hidden module boundary that wants extracting. In this tier the shared prefix IS the module: ARCHITECTURE.md section 17.3 requires every strategy for one LeetCode problem to live in that problem's one solution class, named <Operation>By<Strategy>, so MinTurnsByMutationQueue/MinTurnsByReduceGraph (each with a LeetCode-shaped and a hoisted overload, hence four declarations) all share the operation the problem asks for. Extracting them apart is precisely the split this reorg existed to undo - it is what let the test and the benchmark drift onto different functions. The boundary the check infers is already the file. Scoped to `<Problem>/<Problem>Solution.cs`, which is what that argument covers; the 21 design-tier findings this same entry absorbs charge a broad public surface rather than a prefix, and section 17.3 answers those too - a design problem's strategies cannot be static methods, because LeetCode's published API for such a problem is a stateful object whose operation set is fixed by the problem statement rather than by this repo, so each strategy is a whole class with a constructor. The finding counts declarations per file, so it necessarily sums across the strategies 17.3 requires to be in that one file.

The constructor is deliberately private: HammingGraph's invariant is that every one-character-apart pair among its nodes is already wired, which only Build establishes. A C# primary constructor is always as accessible as its type, so taking the check's advice would expose a second construction path that produces an unwired graph and silently reports no neighbours. The fields exist to keep that door shut, not because the constructor is boilerplate.

The constructor is deliberately private: EdgeGraph's invariant is that every `EdgeGraphNode` in `Nodes` already carries its half of the input edge list, which only Build establishes - Build allocates the nodes and appends each edge to both endpoints' `Edges`. The constructor receives the nodes, never the wiring, so a primary constructor would expose a second construction path whose nodes all have empty `Edges` and the Dijkstra walk silently reports every vertex unreachable, so no edge is ever marked as lying on a shortest path. The constructor exists to keep that door shut, not because it is boilerplate.

The constructor is deliberately private: AppleNetwork's invariant is that every `AppleNode` already carries the roads incident to it in both `ForwardEdges` (weight = cost) and `ReturnEdges` (weight = cost * tax), which only Build establishes - Build allocates the nodes and `AddRoad` appends to both endpoints of every road. The constructor receives the nodes and the prices, never the wiring, so a primary constructor would expose a second construction path whose nodes have no edges and both searches silently report every city as unreachable. The constructor exists to keep that door shut, not because it is boilerplate.

The constructor is deliberately private: PowerStateGraph's invariant is that every `(node, remainingPower)` state in `States` already carries its outgoing transitions, one per power level the signal can still afford, which only Build establishes - Build allocates the whole state table and `WireEdges` fills each state's `Edges`. The constructor receives the table, never the transitions, so a primary constructor would expose a second construction path whose states all have empty `Edges` and the search silently reports the target unreachable no matter how much power it was given. The constructor exists to keep that door shut, not because it is boilerplate.

The constructor is deliberately private: RequiredPathsGraph's invariant is that `Forward[i]` and `Reverse[i]` are the same vertex in the two orientations, each already carrying its incident edges, which only Build establishes - one pass over the input edges allocates both arrays and appends to both. The constructor receives two node arrays, never the correspondence or the wiring, so a primary constructor would expose a second construction path whose arrays are unrelated or unwired and every distance query silently returns infinity. The constructor exists to keep that door shut, not because it is boilerplate.

The constructor is deliberately private: ProbabilityGraph's invariant is that `Nodes[i].Edges` and `Adjacency[i]` describe the same incident edges, one carrying -log(probability) and the other the raw probability, which only Build establishes - Build constructs the instance and then calls `Connect` per input edge to record both views. The constructor receives only the allocated, still-empty containers, so a primary constructor would expose the half-built state as a construction path and both strategies would silently answer as if the graph had no edges. The constructor exists to keep that door shut, not because it is boilerplate.

The constructor is deliberately private: RaceCarStateGraph's invariant is that every `(position, speed)` node in `nodesByState` already carries its 'A' and 'R' successors, which only Build establishes - Build fills the dictionary over the whole bounded box and `WireCommands` gives every node its successors. The constructor receives the dictionary and the speed list, never the successors, so a primary constructor would expose a second construction path whose nodes have empty `Neighbors` and the BFS silently reports the target unreachable. The constructor exists to keep that door shut, not because it is boilerplate.

The constructor is deliberately private: SubdividedGraph's invariant is that every node already carries its incident edges with the subdivided weight `cnt + 1` already folded in, which only Build establishes - Build allocates the nodes and appends each edge to both endpoints. The constructor receives the nodes, never the wiring, so a primary constructor would expose a second construction path whose nodes have empty `Edges` and the reachability count silently reports every original node as unreachable. The constructor exists to keep that door shut, not because it is boilerplate.

The constructor is deliberately private: VisitStateGraph's invariant is that every `(node, mask)` state already carries the successors its input edges allow, and that `StartNodes` holds the n states the walk may begin in, which only Build establishes - Build wires the whole state dictionary and then selects the start states out of that same dictionary. A primary constructor would expose a second construction path that takes a start array and a full mask with no states behind them, and the BFS silently reports no walk that visits every node. The constructor exists to keep that door shut, not because it is boilerplate.

The constructor is deliberately private: ConsecutiveRunGraph's invariant is that every `(node, runLength)` state in `States` already carries the transitions the input edges permit under the length-k rule, which only Build establishes - Build allocates the whole n * k state table and `WireEdges` fills each state's `Edges`. The constructor receives the table, never the transitions, so a primary constructor would expose a second construction path whose states all have empty `Edges` and the search silently reports the target unreachable. The constructor exists to keep that door shut, not because it is boilerplate.

The constructor is deliberately private: RemainderGraph's invariant is that the k remainders form the functional graph the search walks, each node wired to `(r * 10 + 1) % k`, and that `Start` and `Zero` are two nodes of that same graph, which only Build establishes - Build fills the remainder dictionary, wires every node, and then takes both endpoints out of it. The constructor receives only those two nodes, never the cycle behind them, so a primary constructor would expose a second construction path where the repunit search silently reports that no such number exists. The constructor exists to keep that door shut, not because it is boilerplate.

Scoped to `<Problem>/<Problem>Solution.cs` rather than the whole tier because that is exactly what it describes: measured over the 321 solution files it covers, every one declares its top-level type `static class`, so the solution class itself holds no instance state - the state the metric clusters is a nested strategy type's own private state, never shared between arms. ARCHITECTURE.md section 17.3 requires every strategy for one problem to sit in that problem's one solution class, and independent strategies for the same question share nothing BY CONSTRUCTION - that independence is the point, it is what makes them comparable arms. Splitting them into distinct types would recreate exactly the separation section 17.1 documents as the defect (the test and the benchmark each holding their own copy of the algorithm). Fires once per migrated problem on the convention working as designed. The two Harness types that also fired are not solution classes and carry entries of their own.

Not a solution class: it is the one place that discovers every registered problem in the assembly and exposes the result to both harnesses. ARCHITECTURE.md 17.7 gives the harnesses exactly two jobs, assertions and workload sizing, and both must read the same discovered index - so the registry builds it once (Discover/DescribeAll/IsRegistration behind the Lazy BySlug) and projects it twice (CaseArms/WorkloadArms). Measured on a copy: the metric's two clusters are the index accessors (BySlug/All/Get) and the two projections, which reach the index through All rather than by touching the Lazy field, and deleting either side collapses the finding to zero. Both halves are the tier's one subject, the registered problems, and 17.1 names the split this check recommends as the defect it undid.

Not a solution class: it is the typed half of LeetCodeProblem, holding one registration's lookup tables and answering the two operations the harnesses call over them. Measured on a copy: the metric's two clusters are the four published accessors (TitleSlug/StrategyNames/CaseNames/WorkloadArms) and the two operations (RunCase/BindWorkload), and deleting either side collapses the finding to zero. They are one subject - the accessors are what the registry enumerates and RunCase/BindWorkload are what the harnesses call on the enumerated arms; a problem that could be listed but not run, or run but not listed, is not one a harness can use. Resolve sits between them deliberately, taking the dictionary it searches as a parameter, which is what lets one helper serve both call sites rather than a sign of two responsibilities.

Not a naming-convention exemption: the check accepts this repo's ordinary `Member_Scenario_Expectation` test names (DataStructures/Heap/Heap.cs passes with them). It fires here because a solution file is <Name>Solution.cs while its harness is <Name>Tests.cs under Tests/LeetCodeCoverage/, so the file names do not correspond. The coverage itself is complete by construction - ARCHITECTURE.md 17.7 requires one test method per strategy, so every public strategy is asserted against LeetCode's published examples. Waived on the file-name correspondence alone; renaming 780+ harness folders to satisfy it would be churn, not coverage.

BenchmarkDotNet discovers benchmark types by reflection and only accepts a benchmark class that is both public and unsealed - sealing one, or narrowing it to internal, makes BDN drop every benchmark method in it silently, with no error and no warning. Verified empirically on this repo: adding `sealed` to AddBinaryBenchmarks removed both of its benchmarks from `--list flat`, and removing the keyword put them back. There is therefore no honest rewrite for these two checks in a benchmark class: the accessibility and the sealedness are the harness contract, not a design choice.

Re-measured against the unsuppressed source, this family of entries - this glob plus the per-file entries beside it, which share its argument - covers 200 findings in two families. An earlier draft of this reason claimed all of them were field handles, which was wrong for 27 of them. (a) 173 are a BenchmarkDotNet workload handle: a private field of a benchmark class whose type has no buildable empty value (a whole-repo pass substituting the parameterless constructor at all 182 of these sites was refused by the compiler at all 182 -- CS0144 for the interfaces, CS1729 and CS7036 for the types that require arguments), so there is no expression that states the field's empty value because the type has none. What makes those promises true is the benchmark lifecycle this project's benchmark classes all declare, verified file by file: the field is assigned in [GlobalSetup] (or [IterationSetup]) and no [Benchmark] method can run before that assignment, so between construction and Setup the field is never read. (b) The other 27 are not field handles and were each read on its line: 12 are a fixture builder returning the list or tree its own loop just filled (return dummy.Next! and return head! in the Setup-invoked BuildList, return tree.Root!, return _recursiveResult!.Value); 8 unwrap a solution's own result inside the measured method (CloneGraphBenchmarks' CloneByDictionaryDfs(_graph)!.Value, IncreasingOrderSearchTreeBenchmarks' IncreasingBstByRecursiveRelink(BuildTree())!.Value); 7 are the walk step of a method whose input the setup just built (node = node.Next!, node = node.Left ?? node.Right!, _root = tree.Root!). The alternative remedies were weighed and rejected on the code's own terms rather than on convenience: handling the absent case at the point of use would put a null test inside a method whose measured cost is the thing being reported, so the check would make the benchmark measure something other than the algorithm; and an accessor property that throws would restate one BenchmarkDotNet guarantee at each of the 182 sites the constructor pass covered, in 137 files, adding a member to each. The promise is stated where the field is declared and repeated in each file's Setup method, both of which a reader can check without leaving the file.

Almost every finding under this project falls into one of six families, each checked rather than assumed, and in none of them would a name do the work the rule asks a name to do - state what the value MEANS, so a reader stops having to recognise it. (1) Positional indices into a fixed-shape array that LeetCode's own input format defines: `(edge[0], edge[1], edge[2])` is (from, to, weight), `(flight[0], flight[1], flight[2])` is (city, city, price), `(sides[0], sides[1], sides[2])` is a triangle - the index IS the slot, and since 0 and 1 are exempt by the rule, naming only the third would give a reader `sides[0], sides[1], SideCIndex`. A literal used as an index appears at 133 sites, not the 63 an earlier draft of this reason estimated. (2) Mathematical identities that the rule's own rationale does not reach, because there is no second meaning to lose: parity (`% 2`), halving (`low + ((high - low) / 2)` is the overflow-safe midpoint, `(n + 1) / 2` a ceiling half), doubling (`2 * i + 1` generates odds, `1 << (2 * index)` the powers of four), the pair-count formula `n * (n - 1) / 2`, and `for (var divisor = 2; divisor * divisor <= value; divisor++)` walking trial divisors from the smallest one above 1. This is the same judgment this ledger records for DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks/ProblemSolutions/MinimumNumberOfMovesToMakePalindromeBenchmarks.cs, where `length / 2` and `length % 2` were found to be 'the mathematical divisor/modulus for half and odd, not an arbitrary business constant'. Counting only the identities named in this sentence and their close cousins gives 188 sites; widening to any arithmetic sitting beside a literal on a line that is not example data gives 331. waivers.reason: every finding this covers is an xUnit test method named by the repo's own `MemberUnderTest_Scenario_Expectation` convention - `Get_ReturnsTheElementAtTheIndex` says "the member `Get`, in this scenario, returns ...". Not documentation debt dodged: this is the check's own exemption, one suffix over. check-public-api-docs exempts a type and all its members when the type's name ends in `Test` or `Tests`, and the exemption's stated reason is that 'a test type is a test and not a public contract, so it and its members are exempt'. A BenchmarkDotNet harness is the same kind of thing one suffix along: its public surface exists because a runner outside the assembly must reach it, not because a caller does. Measured rather than assumed, the 5338 findings this covers are 1102 types named `*Benchmarks`, 3160 `[Benchmark]` methods and 1076 `[Params]` properties, and every one of them sits in a file matching this glob - the only public-api-docs findings anywhere else in the repo were two on DSAExperimentation.LeetCode/Harness/IBoundWorkload.cs, and those were given XML docs instead of a waiver. The `public` is not this repo's choice to make: BenchmarkDotNet generates a second assembly that constructs the benchmark type, assigns each `[Params]` property through its setter, and invokes each `[Benchmark]` method, so AddDigitsBenchmarks' `public int Value { get; set; }` and `public int Arithmetic()` are public because the runner cannot see them otherwise - `private`, `internal` or `static` all fail to build a case. Documentation on any of the three would be read by no one: there is no caller outside the runner, and the report names every row by the benchmark method and its class, so a `<summary>` would restate the identifier the harness already prints. What this shape actually needs is what 1075 of the 1102 files already carry - a class-level comment saying the file is a harness whose arms are the solution's, as AddDigitsBenchmarks does ('Harness only: both arms are AddDigitsSolution's, the same methods AddDigitsTests proves correct') - and check-public-api-docs does not ask for it, since a `//` comment is not XML documentation and the check is right to want a machine-readable contract where a contract exists.

Sibling of the DSAExperimentation.Tests/** entry above, written the same way - measured, not assumed. This project is the repo's newest test tree and holds all 796 of its unsuppressed check-literals findings (DSAExperimentation, DSAExperimentation.LeetCode and DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks each report none once this ledger's own entries for them are set aside), sitting in 17 of its 19 files across 17 problem folders; the two clean files are clean today, and this is the project-shaped glob its sibling already uses. Classified by the line each sits on rather than by taste. 228 are building the operation script a seam test replays - `IntervalOperation.Add(1, 3)`, `RankOperation.Add("brazil", 2)`, `CacheOperation.Put(3, 30)` - where the literal is an argument of a scripted operation and the only name for it would restate that operation's own signature. 302 are the same data one level out, the query array these problems publish (`int[][] queries = [CountWindow(2), CountWindow(3)];`, an opcode-and-range pair per query). 169 are the scenario's payload written as strings: a problem's alphabet, LeetCode 721's own accounts (`["John", "johnsmith@mail.com", "john_newyork@mail.com"]`), a dictionary's words. 97 sit inside an assertion, where the literal is the answer the case proves - `Assert.Equal(10, MinCostByAutomatonArm("abc", words, costs))` against the `words` and `costs` two lines above, whose sum of cheapest spellings is exactly the asserted 10 - or the operation transcript a replay harness compares against. 157 distinct tokens carry all 796 of them: 37 numeric and 120 string. Naming an assertion's expected value is the shape that is actively harmful rather than merely unnecessary, for the reason the sibling entry gives: `Assert.Equal(20, MinCostByKruskalArm(points))` states the case's answer, and lifting it into a constant makes the test compare a constant with itself. The one family a reader might reach for is the single `precision: 6` at ApplyDiscountEveryNOrders/CashierHashMapCatalogSeamTests.cs:68, and that is already written with xUnit's own parameter name at the call site - the constant it invites would restate `precision` as `DecimalPlaces`, so the name is already there, one character in front of the number.

Every flagged site in this project, measured rather than assumed - and this is the first run of the rule here: the C# front end for `nestedcall` did not exist until recently (its own source records it as GATED, with every `.cs` file answering OUTCOME_UNSUPPORTED before that), so these 333 findings are the whole population and not a residue of earlier work. The rule's entire judgment is a call carrying more than one position handed straight to another call, and in a fixture test that describes two shapes: 187 pass the fixture and the subject's answer into an assertion, and 111 pass the fixture into the harness's answer formatter, `AnswerText.Of(DigitGridWorkloads.BuildGrid(Size, Seed))` (the remaining 35 go into a render or count helper of the same harness - `InOrderValues`, `Values`, `Nodes`, `AnswerSum`, `ExpectedIslandCount`). 74 of the 333 are the two sides of one assertion, the reproducibility pin, `Assert.Equal(AnswerText.Of(X.BuildGrid(Size, Seed)), AnswerText.Of(X.BuildGrid(Size, Seed)))` - and that is the shape where the rule's remedy is not merely unnecessary but wrong: the two sides are deliberately two independent builds of the same input, so a named local is either the same call named twice or one side compared with itself, and the two evaluations have to stay two evaluations because that is the whole content of the test. For the rest the harm the rule names (the value has no name, a debugger has nowhere to stop) is answered by the assertion: xUnit prints the actual value beside the expected one, with the line, at the only moment the value matters, and the intermediate is never read by a later statement - it cannot be, since it sits inside an assertion or a formatter argument. 254 of the 333 sit in an expression-bodied test, the shape this repo's tests use for a one-statement body, so naming the value means rewriting the test as a two-statement block rather than adding a line to it. waivers.reason: no file in this repo can produce this finding truthfully: DSA is an algorithms practice library with no database, no ORM and no data-access dependency anywhere in it - the whole repository declares five package references (BenchmarkDotNet, coverlet.collector, Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk, xunit, xunit.runner.visualstudio), and a scan for SqlConnection, DbConnection, IDbConnection, DbCommand, Npgsql, SqlClient, EntityFramework, DbContext, Dapper, MySql, Sqlite, ConnectionString and OracleConnection over every .cs file finds nothing. What fires here is the check's universal SQL slice, and its front end sets that from the CALLEE NAME ALONE: `csharp_query_methods` (language-kernels/programming/csharp/csharplang/csharp_sql.go) is a flat map of Dapper's own method names - Query, QueryFirst, QuerySingle, QueryMultiple, Execute, ExecuteScalar, ExecuteReader, FromSqlRaw and their Async forms - and `CSharpLanguage.Loop_Calls` sets `Is_Sql: csharp_query_methods[method]` with no receiver check at all, so any in-loop call whose short name is `Query` is reported as a database round trip whatever it is called on. All 33 findings are this repo's own range query: the segment tree, the lazy segment tree, the Fenwick tree, the interval-set and the 2D prefix-sum table each expose a `Query(low, high)` (or the checker/strategy facade over one), and every one of them is O(log n) or O(1) over memory the file already holds - the enclosing loop is the algorithm's outer pass and the query is its inner lookup, which is the structure doing its job rather than a round trip the loop pays for. There is no escape to configure: `boundary_in_loop.calls` only WIDENS what is flagged, so listing nothing keeps this slice, and the rule's own `n-plus-one: allow` marker is unhonoured under this repository's default `safety-only` marker policy - the same reason the nested-call entries above are ledger entries rather than markers. SCOPE: written over `**` because the claim that makes it truthful is about the whole repository being database-free, and it covers the name-collision class rather than `Query` alone, since a future `Execute(...)` in a loop would fire identically; if DSA ever takes a data-access dependency this entry must be retired rather than renewed, and the `expires` date is the backstop. 33 findings across 31 files today - 27 in DSAExperimentation.LeetCode/ (ConstructQuadTree, CountIncreasingQuadruplets, CountSubarraysWithFixedBounds twice, FallingSquares, FindXValueOfArrayII, FruitsIntoBasketsIII, HandlingSumQueriesAfterUpdate, LengthOfTheLongestIncreasingPath, LongestBalancedSubarrayII, LongestIncreasingSubsequenceII twice, LongestSubstringOfOneRepeatingCharacter, MaximumAreaRectangleWithPointConstraintsII, MaximumSumOfSubsequenceWithNonAdjacentElements, MaximumSumQueries, MinimumDeletionsToMakeAlternatingSubstring, MinimumNumberOfCoinsForFruits, MinimumStabilityFactorOfArray, NumberOfLongestIncreasingSubsequence twice, NumberOfPairsAfterIncrement, NumberOfPeopleAwareOfASecret, RangeSumQuery2DImmutable, ReversePairs, ShortestPathInAWeightedTree, SubarraysDistinctElementSumOfSquaresII, ThresholdMajorityQueries), 2 in DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks/ProblemSolutions/ (OnlineMajorityElementInSubarrayBenchmarks, StreamOfCharactersBenchmarks) and 3 in DSAExperimentation.Tests/ (DataStructures/LazySegmentTree/BuildCombineTests, LeetCodeCoverage/OnlineMajorityElementInSubarray/OnlineMajorityElementInSubarrayTests, LeetCodeCoverage/StreamOfCharacters/StreamOfCharactersTests).

The remedy this check ranks first is an interface with a named method, and C# has no lambda-to-interface conversion: `wire` arrives as a lambda at all 8 call sites (GroupAdjacency, CityGraph, GardenNetwork, MinimumEdgeTogglesOnATreeSolution, ToggleTree, BranchNetwork, DislikeAdjacency, DislikeGraph), and a one-method interface cannot be satisfied by one - so the interface would cost a hand-written adapter type in each of those 8 unrelated problem files to express what a delegate already expresses. The declaration is already the check's SECOND-ranked form rather than the third (a named delegate, not a bare `Func`), and it is the one place the contract can be stated: the 7-line comment above it names each parameter (`slot`, `farId`, `farSlot`, `edgeIndex`) and records why both endpoints travel together and why the caller's own edge list is the only place an index can be read from. What it is FOR is also named where a caller meets it: `Build<TSlot>` calls `wire` twice per edge, once from each endpoint, which is what the delegate's shape has to support.

A test-local catalogue factory rather than a slot in production code: `priceOf` is the only callable in the file and the whole of what `Catalogue` varies along with the product count. Every one of its 5 call sites names it (`Catalogue(products: 12, priceOf: product => product * 7)`), so the reading this rule wants a type to supply - what the callable is FOR - is at the call site in the argument's own name. The remedy would need a strategy type for one lambda in one test file, and C# cannot satisfy an interface with a lambda, so it would replace `priceOf: product => product * 7` with a type declared beside it and instantiated at each site: more surface for a reader of the seam test, and the mapping (a product number to its price) would still live in the body a named argument already introduces.

check-responsibility-extraction's own doc (shared-prefix-signals-a-hidden-module.md) calls a prefix cluster a review rather than an automatic defect - a strong signal, not proof - and asks whether the shared prefix names a real responsibility before extracting. Both clusters it counts here are this one file's subject: `Smaller...` and `Greater...` are the boundary VALUE RELATIONS the file is named for, and its header records why all four live together - a problem that needs a tie to belong to one of two equal positions asks for the strict relation on one side and the or-equal one on the other, and that asymmetry (not the scan) is what ApplyOperationsToMaximizeScore's (i - left[i]) * (right[i] - i) is built on; all four are here because that pairing is the reason the sweep is worth writing once, and a caller reaching for a fifth is describing a different algorithm. The four share one private Sweep, so extracting `Smaller` and `Greater` into separate files would separate each relation from the sweep that implements all four and from the sibling it is defined against (strict vs or-equal is the difference between two of these methods and nothing else in the file), and dropping the prefix would take the relation's own name off the method a caller reaches for. Same shape as Manacher.cs's entry above: the prefix names the one algorithm's inseparable halves, not a boundary nobody drew.

The 4 counted declarations are two overload pairs of one operation, and `Shuffled` is the operation's own name rather than a hidden module: each pair is (count, seed) and (count, Random), and the two pairs are the 0-based and 1-based sequences, so the two axes a caller picks independently are handled by arity here instead of by a strategy parameter. The file's own header records why both random forms exist, and it is not an accident of taste: a harness that draws further values after the shuffle (RobotCollisions' healths and directions) must keep ONE stream, because handing it a fresh Random would change every draw after the shuffle and with it the workload a recorded benchmark artifact was measured against - so the Random overload is what makes that possible and the seed overload is the convenience over it. The private helper all four delegate to is `Shuffled(int[] values, Random random)`, the Fisher-Yates pass, so the prefix is already the name of the one algorithm in the file and the public forms are its argument permutations. Splitting the 0-based pair from the 1-based pair would separate a shared shuffle from nothing it shares.

The shared prefix is another check's requirement and the problem's own word, so it is neither accidental nor extractable. `Can` opens a boolean predicate because the question these arms answer IS yes/no (LC 365 canMeasureWater, LC 464 Can I Win, LC 810 xorGame, LC 1927 sumGame all publish a boolean), and check-boolean-predicate requires exactly that: a bool-returning member whose name does not open with is/has/can/should/try is reported. So renaming these arms to break the cluster makes the sibling check fire, and for LC 365 and LC 464 it would also take the name away from the API LeetCode publishes. The prefix is also the problem's own title for one of them: in CanIWinBenchmarks the third counted declaration is the harness type, named for the problem's published title. The locality the check reads as a hidden module is 17.3's requirement read back: every arm for one problem lives in that problem's one benchmark class, next to the `[Benchmark]` attributes that make the arms comparable (the design-tier half of this same argument is the entry for DSAExperimentation.LeetCode/*/*Solution.cs above).

The locality is deliberate, and the rule's own remedy text routes that case here. These are 17.9 companion tests, whose reference answer must be derived independently of the arm under test, and the sections the metric counts are the steps of that one derivation rather than groups that happen to be separated by blank lines. DeleteNodeInALinkedList's Replay follows the arm step for step - its comment says it Mirrors the arm exactly: rebuild the run, target the node at Length/2 and splice it out through the solution the arm calls - so its stanzas are what a reader puts beside the arm's body; splitting them into BuildRun/AdvanceToMiddle/Collect would turn a 31-line mirror into four helpers that have to be reassembled to compare. ImplementQueueUsingStacks' ReferenceFifoSum is one for-loop whose 3-way branch IS the reference simulation (roll, push, pop-and-sum, all sharing the loop variable and the RNG), so each section is a branch of the loop rather than a unit that can be lifted out of it. NumberOfIslands' ExpectedIslandCount is seed-the-mask / count-the-starts / flood / return, with the flood already extracted as FloodFrom(grid, visited, row, col) - the residual section is the two-line preamble and the return.

The counted block in each of these five files is the body of the reference's own traversal loop: dequeue a node, record it, enqueue its children (FindModeInBinarySearchTree's Nodes, ConstructBinaryTreeFromInorderAndPostorderTraversal's LevelOrderValues), the mask-to-subset expansion inside the enumeration loop (SubsetsII's ExpectedMultisetPowerSet), the frontier drain (SurroundedRegions' ExpectedCapture, SwimInRisingWater's IsJoiningCorners). Each is the algorithm the reference IS, written in plain BCL types (Queue<T>, List<T>, HashSet<T>) rather than through the structures under test, so a bug in the tier cannot be shared by the reference - and naming the loop body would name the algorithm's own step after the algorithm. IsJoiningCorners is the clearest case: its block carries the loop's own early `return true` when the far corner is reached, so it is not self-contained at all - the success condition lives in the loop that tests it. The pieces that ARE separable were already lifted: VisitIfOpen and CaptureUnreachedOpenCells (SurroundedRegions), VisitIfLowEnough (SwimInRisingWater), AnswerText.Of and WorkloadValues (SubsetsII), CountNodes (FindModeInBinarySearchTree) all sit beside these bodies as private static helpers.

Already decomposed where decomposition is real: every separable step of this digit-count DP is a named member of this problem's own algebra - FactorialTable.Build(num.Length), FoldDigitSplits(counts, evenSlots, half, table), table.Factorial(evenSlots) and table.Factorial(oddSlots), ModularArithmetic.Modulo - so what remains inline is the digit histogram (a 3-statement loop over a local array), the odd-total rejection, the three locals the DP is handed, and the one-expression return. The metric reports 24 lines, which is this check's own Minimum_Body_Lines: at the soft length the rule is a length signal looking for a piece to NAME, and the nameable pieces of this method have already been named elsewhere in the file.

The counted block is the body of the scan over later rectangles, and it is not self-contained: it contains the loop's own early exit (`if (widthBound <= bestSide) { break; }`), which IS the pruning argument the method exists for - the width bound only shrinks as q advances, so once it can no longer beat the best square found so far, neither can any later q. Lifting the block out would move that break out of the loop it governs (leaving a sentinel or a flag to re-test) and would need the pivot rectangle, both corner arrays, the order, the bound and the running best, which is past this same phase's parameter-count limit. What could be named is the width/height/side triple, three one-expression locals each read once; the method is 27 lines with the scan, the bound and the early exit each explained by the comment directly above it.

One merge's parts, not three responsibilities. Combine is ICombineOperation<RunSegment>'s witness, and the two leading guards are the identity legs that witness owes (`Identity => RunSegment.Empty`, so combining with the empty run must return the other side); the sections after them are the four fields one merge derives and the RunSegment it constructs. The arithmetic that IS separable is already extracted beside it: BridgedPrefixLength and BridgedSuffixLength, each a one-expression helper with its own comment explaining which side's run extends past the boundary. What remains inline is one expression per output field over the two edge characters and the total length, exactly the quantities the file's header records as the whole of what the merged value may depend on (which is also why it is associative), so a further split would name the fields of a single return.

The concept the remedy asks to encapsulate is already encapsulated, and what the metric matched is the one-line call to it: `BuildHarness()` (see the helper at the bottom of each file), which the second test of a mirrored pair has to call for itself. Sharing one harness across the pair is not available - a harness is a [GlobalSetup] benchmark object whose arms mutate the object they are called on, and 17.9 requires each DIRECTION of an arm comparison to be its own named test so that a failure names the direction that disagreed. Measured: in MatrixCellsInDistanceOrderBenchmarksTests the two bodies are mirror images rather than copies - line 41 reads Assert.Equal(AnswerText.Of(DistancesOf(byGridBfs)), AnswerText.Of(DistancesOf(byFormula))) and its sibling at line 53 swaps the two arguments, and the two local names swap with them; MergeKSortedListsBenchmarksTests is the same pair with the arms FlattenSort and MergeByHeap swapped between the two bodies. Extracting the prologue would remove the call that names which harness the test builds while leaving the mirrored assertions where they are.

What the metric matched is the shape of a test's own input rather than a reusable unit: its normalization collapses the literals, and every script in this file is an alternation of the seam's two operations (Add, Count, Add, Count...) because that IS the minimum probe of an interval-count arm - the problem publishes two operations, so a script that reads a count after adding ranges is alternating them by construction. The scripts are the test data: the two the metric paired open with the same two operations (a range, then a count) and diverge immediately after, and the reader compares that literal against the test's own name (overlapping and adjacent adds; repeated and single-integer ranges). Hoisting it would replace a literal with a helper whose argument is the whole test, and the count assertions above each script (which are what the test varies) would stay behind.

The metric's premise is that a type's methods and fields cluster around state they share, and the classes it reports here are the two kinds of type that have no state to share. The `*Tests` classes are xUnit fixtures: xUnit constructs a fresh instance for every test method and the tier's rule is that no test may depend on another, so every helper and every assertion in one of these classes works over locals it was handed - 'clusters that share no state' is not a finding about the class, it is the property the framework requires. The one non-test type in the glob, AnswerText.cs, is an `internal static class`: a namespace for one operation (`Of` and its overloads) and its set form (`OfUnorderedSet`), all pure functions of their arguments, which is why the metric sees no state - there is none to see. Splitting a `*Tests` class would also break the 1:1 subject-to-test-class correspondence this tier is built on and that check-test-coverage reads (one `XTests` for each harness type, named for its subject), and splitting a static helper would put the tier's one way of rendering an answer into comparable text in two files that every harness calls together.

Same fact as the entry for DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks.Tests above: the metric's premise is that a type's methods and fields cluster around state they share, and every class it reports in this project is an xUnit fixture - `sealed partial class ...SeamTests` - where xUnit constructs a fresh instance per test and the tier's rule is that no test depends on another. So each `[Fact]` and each private helper works over locals it was handed, and 'clusters that share no state' describes the framework's contract rather than a hidden responsibility. The class-per-seam naming is what check-test-coverage attributes coverage by (test class plus method name), so splitting one of these would break the correspondence between a seam and the class that proves it.

The check's premise is that a bool beside a same-typed position can be transposed by a caller without the compiler objecting, and the 7 sites it reports in this project are all one shape: a test-local `Replay`/`BuildGraph` helper whose bool sits beside a parameter of a DIFFERENT type, measured one by one - `Replay(IntervalOperation[] script, bool useIntervalSet)` (IntervalSetCountSeamTests.cs:127), `Replay(StreamOperation[] script, bool useIntervalSet)` (IntervalSetSummarySeamTests.cs:146), `Replay(RangeOperation[] script, bool useIntervalSet)` (IntervalSetRangeModuleSeamTests.cs:141), `Replay(RankOperation[] script, bool useTwoHeaps)` (TwoHeapRankSeamTests.cs:137), `BuildGraph(int[][] points, bool oneSided)` (KruskalMstSeamTests.cs:167), `Replay(int capacity, CacheOperation[] script, bool usePrimitive)` (LruCacheEvictionSeamTests.cs:132) and `Replay(int[] nums, NumArrayOperation[] script, bool useSegmentTree)` (SegmentTreePointUpdateRangeSumSeamTests.cs:128). An operation array, an int capacity or a point list is never the same type as a bool, so every transposition a caller could write fails to compile and the hazard this rule names cannot occur at any of the 7. The rule's other stated concern, that a position does not name itself, is answered where it arises: every call site in these 7 files passes the flag as a NAMED argument (`Replay(script, useIntervalSet: true)`, `Replay(capacity, script, usePrimitive: false)`, `BuildGraph(points, oneSided: true)`), so the reader is told what the position means at the point of use. Each flag also selects which of two NAMED strategies the helper replays - IntervalSetCountSeamTests' `Replay` branches to `CreateByIntervalSetMerge` or `CreateByHashSetPerInteger` - so the choice is already spelled at both the arm and the call site, and a two-member enum would relabel that same single position without changing the contract. That is the same judgment the ledger already records for PeakGapNode.Leaf (a bool beside a distinct `int`) and for FlipCountOperation's bool positions inside an interface-fixed signature.

`AssertQuery(int[] query, bool isRangeCount)` (:59) is this project's one site, and it has the LeetCode.Tests shape: the bool's neighbour is an `int[]`, a distinct type, so a transposed call cannot compile. Its only call site (:46) passes `index % QueryKindAlternationCycle == 0` rather than a bare literal, so the call site the check renders as `AssertQuery(query, true)` is not what the source says - the condition states itself. The bool is LeetCode's own two query type codes, which this file already names as RangeCountKind and PointUpdateKind and reads back at :61 and :63, so a two-member enum passed to the helper would be a third spelling of that wire format rather than a name that was missing.

`DifferingPositions(left, right)` (:66) counts the positions where two equal-length strings differ - Hamming distance, a metric, so d(a, b) == d(b, a) and a transposed call returns the same count rather than a silently wrong one. The hazard the rule names cannot occur for a symmetric count. One call site, at :50 and in this file, comparing consecutive values of the chain the fixture builds, where the count is asserted equal to the one-character mutation the chain promises. This is the same judgment the ledger already records for HammingGraph.IsOneApart and WordsWithinTwoEditsOfDictionary.IsWithinEditBudget. The message is narrowed to the function and its arity rather than its parameter names, so renaming a position cannot silently un-waive the finding.

deliberately flat, one-folder-per-LeetCode-problem layout - the same deliberate flatness this ledger already accepts for DSAExperimentation.LeetCode and DSAExperimentation.Tests/LeetCodeCoverage. Each of the 17 subfolders holds exactly one `...SeamTests.cs` and the root holds only the .csproj: the folder names the problem (its external contract, the only name a reader can look it up by) and the file names the internal seam being proved (LruCacheEvictionSeamTests, ReverseTimeUnionSeamTests, TwoHeapRankSeamTests), so the flat list IS the index of which of the 1108 solutions has a named internal structure proven directly rather than through its public answer. This project is the only assembly both DSAExperimentation and DSAExperimentation.LeetCode declare InternalsVisibleTo for, so a folder here is the one place a solution's internals can be reached at all; the 17 folders are not a subsystem this repo owns the shape of, but 17 independent proofs against 17 named, numbered external problems, and grouping them under intermediate categories would be a second hand-maintained taxonomy that can disagree with the tier tree the solutions themselves live in.
